blocks.text: Permission is initially granted for the Diwali congregation at Amritsar, and officials set terms meant to turn the gathering into a manageable arrangement rather than an outright prohibition. The page records this fragile accommodation as a moment when Mughal power appears willing to tolerate Panthic assembly under supervision.

Money quickly becomes part of the political calculation. A ten thousand rupees tax is fixed in connection with the gathering, and while invitations spread through the Khalsa, hostile advisers work to persuade Lahore that armed Sikhs will never remain quiet once assembled in strength.

What begins as permission therefore turns into a trap. Troops move into position, confidence drains away, and a once-hopeful fair becomes a site of looming confrontation in which peace is increasingly difficult to preserve.
